answer:
Start from characters plus an end-of-word marker. Repeatedly count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent pair, and preserve merge order as ranks. Inference applies those learned merges in rank order, never relearns counts on the new word. Lexicographic tie-breaking gives repeatable training. This educational implementation has no byte fallback; production tokenizers additionally define normalization, pretokenization, unknown-token behavior, and offsets.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** If the most frequent adjacent pair is $(a,b)$, training replaces its nonoverlapping occurrences by a new symbol and records that merge's rank. At inference, the lowest-ranked applicable learned merge wins. This distinction between learning pair frequencies and applying fixed ranks is essential for deterministic tokenization and compatibility with a trained embedding table. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06226)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter6/5) and [2](https://github.com/karpathy/minbpe).
